Start by always testing your queries against the new planner before you upgrade.

The new planner in PostgreSQL 15 can choose more efficient paths for large joins.

For example,
 an analyst running a month‑end report saw the runtime drop from ten minutes to under six minutes after the planner switch.

PostgreSQL 15 also adds native support for logical replication of partitioned tables.

That means you can now replicate data without extra scripts,
 keeping the source and target in sync more reliably.

Another practical win is the improved sort performance thanks to incremental sorting.

If your workloads involve ORDER BY on large tables,
 you’ll notice less CPU pressure and faster results.

The release also bumps up compression for TOAST data,
 reducing storage costs for wide columns.

In practice,
 a data warehouse that stores JSON payloads saved roughly 15 % on disk after the upgrade.

Takeaway: before you schedule the upgrade,
 run a subset of your critical queries on a test cluster with version 15.

Compare execution plans and timings,
 then plan the rollout based on those results.

Doing this simple validation helps avoid surprises and lets you reap the performance gains confidently.
news_posts.source_article: PostgreSQL 15 advances open source relational database - TechTarget

news_posts.post_content:
When you keep adding new data to a language model, you risk forgetting what it already knows.
Google Research recently introduced a “sleep” framework that lets LLMs pause and consolidate knowledge, similar to how humans sleep.
In continual learning, a model is updated repeatedly with fresh information without retraining from scratch.
The problem is “catastrophic forgetting,” where the model’s performance on earlier tasks drops after each update.
The sleep framework adds an offline consolidation step: after a training batch, the model re‑exposes itself to a curated set of past examples.
Fact: The researchers showed that a brief sleep phase improved retention on prior benchmarks by up to 12 %.
Interpretation: This suggests that periodic replay can act like a memory refresher without the cost of full retraining.
A practical checklist for applying sleep in your projects is:
• Define a small, representative subset of historic data to replay.
• After each fine‑tuning session, run a short “sleep” epoch on that subset.
• Measure both new‑task performance and old‑task stability before and after sleep.
• Adjust the replay size or frequency if retention gains plateau.
By keeping the replay set tiny, the extra compute stays modest while still giving the model a chance to reinforce old patterns.
If you’re fine‑tuning an LLM, schedule a short sleep phase after each update to protect prior knowledge.
That simple habit can make your models more reliable over time.

concept_posts.post_content:
A common mistake when adding extensions is installing them directly on a production database without testing first.
You might think the command is harmless,
but it can lock tables,
cause version mismatches,
and even break existing queries.
Example: a team needed spatial queries,
so they ran `CREATE EXTENSION postgis;` on the live DB.
The extension pulled in geometry types,
but the application started failing because some old functions expected plain text.
Here is a quick checklist to avoid that pitfall:
- Verify the PostgreSQL version matches the extension package.
- Test the extension in a staging environment first.
- Review required privileges and dependencies before enabling it.
A frequent oversight is forgetting to grant USAGE on the new schema,
which leaves the extension invisible to users.
Each extension lives in its own schema,
so you can control visibility with search_path.
PostGIS adds geometry types and spatial functions,
while pg_trgm provides fast similarity searches using trigram indexes.
Make sure the extension version aligns with the server's major version to avoid runtime errors.
Rule of thumb: treat every extension like a new library – install, test, and document before it touches production.
What’s the last extension you added, and how did you validate it?
